title: Limits at infinity and asymptotes
section: Limits of Functions as x → ±∞ ▷ End behavior
terms: limit at infinity; horizontal asymptote; vertical asymptote; slant asymptote; oblique asymptote.

exposition.text:
A finite limit f(x) → L as x → +∞ or −∞ gives a horizontal asymptote y = L at that end. A
vertical line x = a is an asymptote if at least one one-sided limit is infinite. A slant asymptote
y = mx + b satisfies f(x) − (mx + b) → 0 at the relevant infinite end. Polynomial division is
especially effective for rational functions.
A zero of a denominator is not automatically a vertical asymptote: a common factor can pro-

duce a removable hole instead. For radicals, x = |x|, so positive and negative infinity often
produce different end behavior. Infinite limits describe growth rather than finite real limits;
matching signs on two sides must be checked separately.

The condition f(x) − (mx + b) → 0 does not imply f (x) → m: a small-amplitude term can have
a rapidly oscillating derivative. Differentiate limits only when a theorem justifies doing so.

The graph of f(x) = (x + 3x + 1)/(x + 1) has which asymptotes?
(A) x = −1 and y = x + 2 (B) x = −1 and y = x + 3
(C) x = 1 and y = x + 2 (D) y = 1 only
(E) y = x + 2 only

solution.text:
Long division gives f (x) = x + 2 − 1/(x + 1). The remainder tends to zero at either infinity,
while the numerator is nonzero at x = −1, producing a genuine pole there.

For f(x) = on its natural domain, which statement is correct?
(x − 1)(x + 2)
(A) Both x = 1 and x = −2 are vertical asymptotes.
(B) Only x = 1 is a vertical asymptote.
(C) Only x = −2 is a vertical asymptote; x = 1 is a removable hole.
(D) Neither excluded point admits a finite or infinite one-sided limit.
(E) The horizontal asymptote is y = 0.

solution.text:
Away from the exclusions the function equals (x − 1)/(x + 2). At 1 it has finite limit zero,
allowing a continuous extension. At −2 the numerator tends to −3 and the denominator to
zero, giving a vertical asymptote. At either infinite end the limit is 1.
